body_md:
\label{thm:main-01}
		Suppose $K\in C^\infty(M)$ and
		$h\in C^\infty(\partial M)$ are two positive functions and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:intro-critical-parameters}
		\rho+\rho'=2\pi,\qquad \rho>0,\qquad \rho'>0.
	\end{equation}
Suppose that $p\in\partial M$
		is a maximum point of
		$$
		A+\frac{\rho}{\pi}\log K+\frac{\rho'}{\pi}\log h^2
		\qquad\text{on }\partial M.
		$$
		If
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:intro-existence-condition}
			\begin{aligned}
				&-\frac{K_\nu(p)}{K(p)}-2\kappa(p)+
				\frac{2\rho'}{\pi\rho e^{A(p)/2}}\Lambda(G,h)>0,				
			\end{aligned}
		\end{equation} where $\Lambda(G,h)$ is the boundary integration constant defined in \eqref{Def:integration-constant},
		then $J_{\rho,\rho'}$ attains its minimizer in $W^{1,2}(M)$.
		Consequently, \eqref{equation:mean-field} admits a smooth solution.

\label{thm:main-03}
		Let $M$ be the spherical cap above and $K$ be a  smooth
		positive function. Then we have:
\begin{itemize}

\item[(1)] Assume $h$ is a smooth  positive function and \eqref{eq:intro-critical-parameters} holds.
		Suppose that $p\in\partial M$ is a maximum point of
		$$\rho\log K+2\rho'\log h \ \  on \ \ \partial M.$$ If
		\begin{equation}\label{equation:22}
		\frac{K_\nu(p)}{K(p)}+2\cot\theta_0
		+\frac{2\rho'}{\rho}
		\frac{(-\Delta_{\partial M})^{1/2}h(p)}{h(p)}<0,

		\eqref{equation:mean-field} has a smooth solution.

\item[(2)] Assume $h\equiv 0$, $\rho=2\pi,\  \rho'=0$. Suppose that $p\in\partial M$ is a maximum point of
		$K$ on $\partial M$. If
		$$
		\frac{K_\nu(p)}{K(p)}+2\cot\theta_0
		<0,

		then $J_{2\pi,0}$ attains its minimizer and
		\eqref{equation:17} has a smooth solution.

\label{thm:main-06}
	Let $\mathbb D=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:|x|<1\}$ be the standard unit disk.
	Let $K\in C^\infty(\overline{\mathbb D})$ and
	$h\in C^\infty(\partial\mathbb D)$, where $K>0$, $h> 0$ or $h\equiv 0$.
	Denote by $H$ the harmonic extension of $h$, i.e.
	$$
	\begin{cases}
		\Delta H=0,
		&\text{in }\mathbb D,\\
		H=h,
		&\text{on }\partial\mathbb D.
	\end{cases}

	Set
	$$
	\Phi(x)=H(x)+\sqrt{H(x)^2+K(x)},
	\qquad x\in\overline{\mathbb D}.
	$$
	Let $p\in\partial\mathbb D$ be a maximal point of $\Phi(x)$, i.e. $\Phi(p)=\max_{\partial\mathbb D}\Phi$. Suppose
	$$
	\partial_\nu\Phi(p)<0,
	$$

	Then there exists $u\in C^\infty(\overline{\mathbb D})$
	satisfying
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:disk-prescribed-curvature}
		\begin{cases}
			-\Delta u=2Ke^u,
			&\text{in }\mathbb D,\\
			\partial_\nu u+2=2he^{u/2},
			&\text{on }\partial\mathbb D.
		\end{cases}
	\end{equation}

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:normalization-ratio-bounds}
		There exists a constant $C>1$, independent of $\epsilon$, such that
		$$
		C^{-1}\leq\frac{\mu_\epsilon}{\kappa_\epsilon}\leq C
		$$
		for all sufficiently small $\epsilon>0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By the Moser--Trudinger inequalities on compact surfaces with boundary \cite{ChangYang1988,LiLiu2005,Yang2006} and the boundedness of $K,h$, we have
		$$
		J_{2\pi,0}(u)\geq-C,\ \ J_{0,2\pi}(u)\geq-C,
		\qquad u\in W^{1,2}(M).
		$$
		
		Since $\rho_\epsilon+\rho'=2\pi-\epsilon$,
		a direct computation gives
		$$
		\begin{aligned}
			J_{\rho_\epsilon,\rho'}(u_\epsilon)
			={}&
			\left(1-\frac{\epsilon}{2\pi}\right)
			J_{2\pi,0}(u_\epsilon)
			+\frac{\epsilon}{4\pi}
			\int_M|\nabla u_\epsilon|^2\,dv_g+4\rho'
			\log\frac{\mu_\epsilon}{\kappa_\epsilon}\\
			={}&
			\left(1-\frac{\epsilon}{2\pi}\right)
			J_{0,2\pi}(u_\epsilon)
			+\frac{\epsilon}{4\pi}
			\int_M|\nabla u_\epsilon|^2\,dv_g+4\rho_\epsilon
			\log\frac{\kappa_\epsilon}{\mu_\epsilon}.
		\end{aligned}
		$$
		Noting $u_\epsilon$ is a minimizer, then
		$$
		J_{\rho_\epsilon,\rho'}(u_\epsilon)
		\leq
		J_{\rho_\epsilon,\rho'}(0)
		\leq C,
		$$ which implies
		$$
		4\rho'
		\log\frac{\mu_\epsilon}{\kappa_\epsilon}\leq C,
		\qquad
		4\rho_\epsilon
		\log\frac{\kappa_\epsilon}{\mu_\epsilon}\leq C
		$$ when $\epsilon$ is small.
		Since $\rho,\ \rho'\in (0,2\pi)$, then the conclusion of the lemma follows.

title: Lemma
body_md: Setting $\lambda_\epsilon=\max_{x\in M}v_\epsilon(x)$, then $\liminf_{\epsilon\searrow 0}\lambda_\epsilon=+\infty$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If not, there exists a subsequence of $v_{\epsilon}$ (also denoted by itself), such that $\lambda_\epsilon\leq C$. By standard elliptic theory, we get $\|v_\epsilon\|_{L^\infty(M)}\leq C.$

On one hand, by \eqref{equation:liouville-01} and elliptic estimates, there holds $\|v_\epsilon\|_{W^{2,p}(M)}\leq C(p),$ for any $p>1$.	On the other hand, since $2\log \mu_\epsilon$ is a constant, there must be $$-C\leq 2\log \mu_\epsilon \leq 0,$$ which yields $$\|u_\epsilon\|_{L^\infty(M)}\leq C.$$ Otherwise, we have $$u_\epsilon=v_\epsilon+2\log  \mu_\epsilon \to -\infty$$ uniformly in $M$, which is a contradiction to \eqref{equation:03}.
		
		Thus, we obtain $$\|u_\epsilon\|_{W^{2,p}(M)}\leq C(p),$$ for any $p>1$. Then passing to a subsequence, $u_\epsilon\to u$ strongly in $W^{1,2}(M)$, which is also a contradiction.

title: Proof
body_md:
On the one hand, by \cite{Li-Zhu}, we have $$\int_{\mathbb R^2_+}\tilde{K}(0)e^wdx+ \int_{\partial\mathbb R^2_+}\tilde{h}(0)e^{\frac{w}{2}}=4\pi.$$ On the other hand, since $$\int_M Ke^{v_\epsilon}dv_g=1,\ \ \int_{\partial M}\widetilde{h}_\epsilon e^{\frac{v_\epsilon}{2}}ds_g=1,\ \ \rho+\rho'=2\pi,$$ then $$\int_{\mathbb R^2_+}\tilde{K}(0)e^wdx\leq 2\rho,\ \  \int_{\partial\mathbb R^2_+}\tilde{h}(0)e^{\frac{w}{2}}\leq 2\rho',$$ which implies the inequalities in the above estimates must be equalities.
		
		A direct computation yields $$2\rho'=\int_{\partial\mathbb R^2_+}\tilde{h}(0)e^{\frac{w}{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{8}\pi\tilde{h}(0)}{\sqrt{\tilde{K}(0) +\frac{1}{2}\tilde{h}^2(0)}}.$$ That is $$\frac{\tilde{h}^2(0)}{\tilde{K}(0)}=\frac{2\rho'^2}{4\pi^2-\rho'^2}.$$ Then one can  easily get the conclusion of the lemma from the definition of $(\tilde{K}(0),\tilde{h}(0))$.

label: lem:maximum-point-on-boundary
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:maximum-point-on-boundary}
		When $\epsilon>0$ is small enough, there must be
		$
		x_\epsilon\in\partial M.
		$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose the conclusion is false. Then there
		exists a sequence $\epsilon_j\searrow 0$ such that
		$x_{\epsilon_j}\in M\setminus\partial M$. For simplicity of notations, we
		still denote it by $\epsilon$.
		
		In the conformal coordinate system introduced above, identifying $p$
		with the origin, write
		\[
		x_\epsilon=(s_\epsilon,t_\epsilon),
		\qquad
		t_\epsilon>0.
		\]
		Let
		\[
		x_\epsilon^0:=(s_\epsilon,0)\in\partial^0D^+.
		\]
		Since $a=0$, we have
		\[
		\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\frac{t_\epsilon}{\delta_\epsilon}
		=\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}
		\frac{\operatorname{dist}
			\left(x_\epsilon,\partial^0D^+\right)}
		{\delta_\epsilon}
		= 0.
		\]
		Set
		\[
		y_\epsilon
		:=
		\frac{x_\epsilon^0-x_\epsilon}{\delta_\epsilon}
		=
		\left(0,-\frac{t_\epsilon}{\delta_\epsilon}\right).
		\]
		Then $y_\epsilon$ lies on the flat part of
		$\partial\Omega_\epsilon$ and
		$
		y_\epsilon\longrightarrow (0,0).
		$
		
		Since $x_\epsilon$ is an interior maximum point of $v_\epsilon$, we
		have
		$
		\nabla v_\epsilon(x_\epsilon)=0.
		$
		Recalling the definition of $w_\epsilon$, it follows that
		\[
		w_\epsilon(0)=0,
		\qquad
		\nabla w_\epsilon(0)=0.
		\]
		Moreover, the boundary elliptic estimates obtained above imply that
		$
		\left\|w_\epsilon\right\|_
		{C^2(D_1(0)\cap\overline{\Omega_\epsilon})}
		\leq C.
		$
		Therefore, we have
		$$
		\begin{aligned}
			\left|\nabla w_\epsilon(y_\epsilon)\right|
			&=
			\left|
			\nabla w_\epsilon(y_\epsilon)-\nabla w_\epsilon(0)
			\right| \leq
			\left\|D^2w_\epsilon\right\|_
			{L^\infty(D_1(0)\cap\Omega_\epsilon)}
			|y_\epsilon|
			\leq C|y_\epsilon|
			\longrightarrow 0,
		\end{aligned}
		$$
		and
		$$
		\begin{aligned}
			|w_\epsilon(y_\epsilon)|
			&=
			|w_\epsilon(y_\epsilon)-w_\epsilon(0)| \leq
			\left\|\nabla w_\epsilon\right\|_
			{L^\infty(D_1(0)\cap\Omega_\epsilon)}
			|y_\epsilon|
			\leq C|y_\epsilon|
			\longrightarrow 0.
		\end{aligned}
		$$
		In particular,
		$
		\frac{\partial w_\epsilon}{\partial\nu}(y_\epsilon)
		\longrightarrow 0.
		$
		
		On the other hand, the boundary condition satisfied by
		$w_\epsilon$ gives
		$$
		\frac{\partial w_\epsilon}{\partial\nu}(y_\epsilon)
		=
		2\rho'
		\widetilde{h}_\epsilon(x_\epsilon^0)
		e^{\frac{w_\epsilon(y_\epsilon)}{2}}= 2\rho'
			h(x_\epsilon^0)
			\frac{\mu_\epsilon}{\kappa_\epsilon}e^{\frac{w_\epsilon(y_\epsilon)}{2}} \longrightarrow
			2\rho'h(p)
			\sqrt{
				\frac{K(p)}
				{(4\pi-\rho)h^2(p)}
			}
			\neq 0
		$$
		which contradicts
		\[
		\frac{\partial w_\epsilon}{\partial\nu}(y_\epsilon)
		\longrightarrow 0.
		\]
		Consequently, $x_\epsilon\in\partial M$ for all sufficiently small
		$\epsilon>0$.

body_md:
Using the notations as before, then we have $\int_MKe^{v_\varepsilon}\,dv_g=1$ and
	$$
	\begin{cases}
		-\Delta_gv_\varepsilon
		+\dfrac{4\pi-2\varepsilon}{|M|}
		=
		(4\pi-2\varepsilon)Ke^{v_\varepsilon},
		&\text{in }M,\\[6pt]
		\partial_\nu v_\varepsilon=0,
		&\text{on }\partial M.
	\end{cases}
	$$
	
	
	 A similar argument yields that passing to a subsequence, there holds
	$$
	\lambda_\varepsilon
	=
	v_\varepsilon(x_\varepsilon)
	=
	\max_{\overline M}v_\varepsilon\to +\infty,\ \ x_\epsilon\to p\in\partial M,\ \
	\frac{\operatorname{dist}(x_\varepsilon,\partial M)}
	{\delta_\varepsilon}\to a=0,\ \ as\ \ \epsilon\to 0.
	$$
	
	
	In the conformal coordinates used above, write
	$x_\varepsilon=(s_\varepsilon,t_\varepsilon)$ and set
	$$
	w_\varepsilon(x)
	=
	v_\varepsilon(x_\varepsilon+\delta_\varepsilon x)
	+2\log\delta_\varepsilon.
	$$
	Then
	$$
	w_\varepsilon(x)
	\longrightarrow
	w(x)
	=
	-2\log\left(1+\frac{\pi K(p)}2|x|^2\right)
	$$
	in $C^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(\overline{\mathbb R^2_+})$, where $w(x)$ satisfies $$-\Delta w=4\pi K(p)e^w\ \ in\ \ \mathbb R^2_+,\ \ \partial_\nu w=0\ \ on\ \ \partial \mathbb R^2_+.$$
	In particular,
	$$
	w(x)=-2\log\left(1+\frac{\pi K(p)}{2}|x|^2\right),\ \ \int_{\mathbb R^2_+}4\pi K(p)e^w\,dx=4\pi.
	$$
	
	
	Now we claim the conclusion of Lemma~\ref{lem:maximum-point-on-boundary}  still holds.
	
	Otherwise, there exists a sequence
	$\varepsilon\searrow0$ such that $t_\varepsilon>0$. Since
	$$
	\partial_{22}w(0)=-2\pi K(p)<0,
	$$
	by the preceding $C^2$ convergence and the fact
	$t_\varepsilon/\delta_\varepsilon\to0$, we get $$\partial^2_{22}w_\epsilon (0)<-\frac{3}{2}\pi K(p)<0,$$ when $\epsilon$ is small.

Then for any $-\frac{t_\epsilon}{\delta_\epsilon}\leq x_2\leq 0$, we get
\begin{align*}
\partial^2_{22}w_\epsilon(0,x_2)\leq \partial^2_{22}w_\epsilon(0)+\|D^3 w_\epsilon\|_{L^\infty(D_1(0)\cap \overline{\Omega_\epsilon})}\frac{t_\epsilon}{\delta_\epsilon}<-\pi K(p)
\end{align*}when $\epsilon$ is small.

	Therefore, we obtain
	$$
	\begin{aligned}
		0
		&=
		\partial_2w_\varepsilon(0)
		-
		\partial_2w_\varepsilon(0,-\frac{t_\epsilon}{\delta_\epsilon})&=
		\int^0_{-\frac{t_\varepsilon}{\delta_\epsilon}}
		\partial_{22}w_\varepsilon(0,t)\,dt\leq
		-\frac{\pi K(p)t_\varepsilon}{\delta_\varepsilon}
		<0,
	\end{aligned}
	$$
	which is a contradiction. Thus $x_\varepsilon\in\partial M$
	for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon$.
	
	One can check all the remaining proofs in the previous case still work. We finished the proof of Proposition \ref{prop:lower-bound}.

label: equation:05
title: Proof
body_md:
In a normal coordinate system near $p$,
		the Riemannian metric can be written as $g = dr^2 + g^2(r,\theta)d\theta^2$ with
		$$g(r, \theta)=r-\frac{\Pi(p)}{6}r^3+O(r^4).$$
		By the divergence theorem, we have
		\begin{align}\label{equation:05}
			\int_{\partial^+B_r(p)}\frac{\partial G}{\partial\nu}=&\int_{M \backslash B_r(p)}-\Delta G +\int_{\partial M \backslash B_r(p)} \frac{\partial G}{\partial\nu}\notag\\
			=&-\frac{4\pi}{|M|}(|M|-|B_r(p)|)\notag\\
			=&-4\pi+\frac{4\pi}{|M|}\frac{\pi r^2}{2}+o(r^2).
		\end{align}
		On the other hand,
		\begin{align*}
			\int_{\partial^+B_r(p)}\frac{\partial G}{\partial\nu}=\int_{\theta_1(r)}^{\pi-\theta_2(r)}&\left(-\frac{4}{r}+b_1\cos\theta+b_2\sin\theta+2c_1r \cos^2\theta +4c_2r\sin\theta\cos\theta+2c_3 r \sin^2 \theta\right)\\
			&\cdot \left(r-\frac{1}{6}\Pi(p)r^3+O(r^4)\right)d\theta .
		\end{align*}
		
		Let $p=0$ and $x_1,x_2$ be rectangular coordinates on $T_0M$ such that $\frac{\partial}{\partial x_2}$ is the inward unit normal vector to $\partial M$ at $0\in \partial M$. By \cite{Glutsyuk} or Lemma \ref{lem:03} in the appendix, in a small neighborhood of $0$, we can write $\partial M$ as a graph $(x_1, f(x_1))$, where
		$$
		f(x_1)=\frac{1}{2}\kappa x_1^2+\frac{1}{6}\kappa'x_1^3+O(x_1^4)
		$$
		and $\kappa=\kappa(p)$ is the geodesic curvature of $\partial M$ at $p\in \partial M$, $\kappa'=\nabla_\tau\kappa (p)$.
		
		The circle $\partial^+B_r(p)$ intersects $\partial M$ at two points
		$$
		(R_+(r),f(R_+(r)))\quad\mbox{and}\quad
		(-R_-(r),f(-R_-(r))),
		$$
		where $R_+(r),R_-(r)>0$. Then
		$$
		r^2=R_+^2(r)+f^2(R_+(r))
		=R_-^2(r)+f^2(-R_-(r))
		=R_\pm^2(r)+O(R_\pm^4(r)),
		$$
		which implies
		$$
		R_+(r)=r+O(r^3),\qquad R_-(r)=r+O(r^3).
		$$
		For the positive intersection point, we have
		$$
		\tan\theta_1(r)=\frac{f(R_+(r))}{R_+(r)}
		=\frac{1}{2}\kappa R_+(r)+\frac{1}{6}\kappa'R_+^2(r)+O(R_+^3(r))
		=\frac{1}{2}\kappa r+\frac{1}{6}\kappa'r^2+O(r^3),
		$$
		which implies
		$$
		\theta_1(r)=\arctan\left(\frac{1}{2}\kappa r+\frac{1}{6}\kappa'r^2+O(r^3)\right)
		=\frac{1}{2}\kappa r+\frac{1}{6}\kappa'r^2+O(r^3).
		$$
		For the negative intersection point, we have
		$$
		f(-R_-(r))
		=\frac{1}{2}\kappa R_-^2(r)-\frac{1}{6}\kappa'R_-^3(r)+O(R_-^4(r)),
		$$
		and hence
		$$
		\tan\theta_2(r)=\frac{f(-R_-(r))}{R_-(r)}
		=\frac{1}{2}\kappa R_-(r)-\frac{1}{6}\kappa'R_-^2(r)+O(R_-^3(r))
		=\frac{1}{2}\kappa r-\frac{1}{6}\kappa'r^2+O(r^3),
		$$
		which implies
		$$
		\theta_2(r)=\frac{1}{2}\kappa r-\frac{1}{6}\kappa'r^2+O(r^3).
		$$
		Therefore,
		$$
		\theta_1(r)+\theta_2(r)=\kappa r+O(r^3).
		$$
		
		A direct computation yields
		\begin{align*}
			\int_{\theta_1(r)}^{\pi-\theta_2(r)}-\frac{4}{r}\left(r-\frac{1}{6}\Pi(p)r^3+O(r^4)\right)d\theta
			&=(-4+\frac{2}{3}\Pi r^2)(\pi-\theta_1(r)-\theta_2(r))+O(r^3)\\
			&=-4\pi+4\kappa r+\frac{2\pi}{3}\Pi r^2+O(r^3),
		\end{align*}
		\begin{align*}
			&\int_{\theta_1(r)}^{\pi-\theta_2(r)}(b_1\cos\theta+b_2\sin\theta)(r-\frac{1}{6}\Pi(p)r^3+O(r^4))d\theta \\
			&=b_1r(\sin(\pi-\theta_2)-\sin\theta_1)+b_2r(\cos\theta_1-\cos(\pi-\theta_2))+O(r^3)\\
			&=2b_2r+O(r^3)
		\end{align*}
		and
		\begin{align*}
			&\int_{\theta_1(r)}^{\pi-\theta_2(r)}\left(2c_1r \cos^2\theta +4c_2r\sin\theta\cos\theta+2c_3 r \sin^2 \theta\right)\left(r-\frac{1}{6}\Pi(p)r^3+O(r^4)\right)d\theta\\&=(c_1+c_3)\pi r^2+O(r^3).
		\end{align*}
		Therefore,
		\begin{align}\label{equation:04}
			\int_{\partial^+B_r(p)}\frac{\partial G}{\partial\nu}
			=-4\pi+(4\kappa+2b_2)r+
			\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\Pi+c_1\pi+c_3\pi\right)r^2+O(r^3).
		\end{align}
		By comparing \eqref{equation:04} with \eqref{equation:05}, we get
		$$
		b_2=-2\kappa,\qquad
		\frac{2\pi}{3}\Pi+c_1\pi+c_3\pi=\frac{2\pi^2}{|M|}.
		$$

		+A(p)+b_1(p)x_1+b_2(p)x_2\right)
		\right|
		\leq\frac{C}{R_\epsilon}.

			|\nabla_g\phi_{\epsilon,\delta}|^2\,dv_g \notag\\
			&=\frac12\int_{M\cap\{R_\epsilon<r_\epsilon<2R_\epsilon\}}

body_md:
Fix $r_0>0$ sufficiently small so that geodesic normal coordinates
		centered at $p$ are defined in $\{r\leq r_0\}$ and
		$\partial M$ is given by
		$$
		x_2=f(x_1)
		=
		\frac{\kappa(p)}{2}x_1^2+O(|x_1|^3).
		$$
		For $0<s\leq r_0$, let $x_s^-<0<x_s^+$ be the $x_1$-coordinates of
		the two points in $\partial M\cap\{r=s\}$. Since
		$$
		s^2=(x_s^\pm)^2+f(x_s^\pm)^2,
		$$
		we have
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:boundary-intersection-expansion}
			x_s^+=s+O(s^3),
			\qquad
			x_s^-=-s+O(s^3).
		\end{equation}
		
		Denote $h_1=\frac{\partial }{\partial x_1}h(p)$ and $$H(x_1)dx_1:=h(x)e^{G(x,p)/2}\,ds_g-h(p)e^{\frac{1}{2}A(p)}\frac{1+(\frac{1}{2}b_1+\frac{h_1}{h(p)})x_1}{x_1^2}dx_1.$$
		Noting that
		\begin{align*}
			h(x)e^{G(x,p)/2}\,ds_g=h(p)e^{\frac{1}{2}A(p)}\frac{1+(\frac{1}{2}b_1+\frac{h_1}{h(p)})x_1+O(x_1^2)}{x_1^2}\left(1+O(x_1^2)\right)dx_1,\ \ \text{for }\delta\leq r\leq r_0,
		\end{align*}
		then $$|H(x_1)|\leq C(r_0).$$
		We have
		\begin{align*}
			&\int_{\partial M\cap\{\delta\leq r\leq r_0\}}
			h(x)e^{G(x,p)/2}\,ds_g
			-
			\frac{2e^{A(p)/2}h(p)}{\delta}\\ &=h(p)e^{\frac{1}{2}A(p)}\int_{\partial M\cap\{\delta\leq r\leq r_0\}}
			\frac{1+(\frac{1}{2}b_1+\frac{h_1}{h(p)})x_1}{x_1^2}dx_1
			-
			\frac{2e^{A(p)/2}h(p)}{\delta}+ \int_{\partial M\cap\{\delta\leq r\leq r_0\}}H(x_1)dx_1\\
			&=
			e^{A(p)/2}h(p)
			\left[
			\frac1{x_\delta^+}
			-
			\frac1{x_\delta^-}
			-
			\frac2\delta
			-
			\frac1{x_{r_0}^+}
			+
			\frac1{x_{r_0}^-}
			\right]+
			e^{A(p)/2}
			\left(
			h_1+\frac12b_1(p)h(p)
			\right)
			\log
			\frac{x_{r_0}^+|x_\delta^-|}
			{x_\delta^+|x_{r_0}^-|}\\
			&\quad +\int_{\partial M\cap\{\delta\leq r\leq r_0\}}H(x_1)dx_1
		\end{align*}
		
		By \eqref{eq:boundary-intersection-expansion},
		$$
		\frac1{x_\delta^+}
		-
		\frac1{x_\delta^-}
		-
		\frac2\delta
		=
		O(\delta),
		\qquad
		\log\frac{|x_\delta^-|}{x_\delta^+}
		=
		O(\delta^2).
		$$
		
		Hence,
		\begin{align*}
			&\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}
			\left[
			\int_{\partial M\cap\{\delta\leq r\leq r_0\}}
			h(x)e^{G(x,p)/2}\,ds_g
			-
			\frac{2e^{A(p)/2}h(p)}{\delta}
			\right]\\
			&=
			e^{A(p)/2}h(p)
			\left(
			-\frac1{x_{r_0}^+}
			+
			\frac1{x_{r_0}^-}
			\right)+
			e^{A(p)/2}
			\left(
			h_1+\frac12b_1(p)h(p)
			\right)
			\log\frac{x_{r_0}^+}{|x_{r_0}^-|}+\int_{\partial M\cap\{ r\leq r_0\}}H(x_1)dx_1.
		\end{align*}
		The right-hand side depends only on the fixed $r_0$ and is finite.
		Therefore, the above limit exists and is finite.

body_md:
Assume now that
		$$
		M=\mathbb S^2\cap\{x_3\geq\cos\theta_0\},
		\qquad 0<\theta_0<\pi.
		$$
		Using the spherical parametrization
		$$
		x=(\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\sin\theta\sin\varphi,\cos\theta),\ 0\leq\theta\leq\theta_0,\ 0\leq\varphi<2\pi,
		$$
		then
		$$
		g=d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2.
		$$
		Moreover,
		$$
		\begin{aligned}
			\partial M=\{\theta=\theta_0\},\
			|M|=2\pi(1-\cos\theta_0)
			=4\pi\sin^2\frac{\theta_0}{2},\
			ds_g=\sin\theta_0\,d\varphi.
		\end{aligned}
		$$
		The inward unit normal along $\partial M$ is $-\partial_\theta$. Since
		$$
		\nabla_{\frac{1}{\sin\theta_0}\partial_\varphi}
		\left(
		\frac{1}{\sin\theta_0}\partial_\varphi
		\right)
		=
		-\cot\theta_0\,\partial_\theta,
		$$
		the sign convention used above gives
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:spherical-cap-kappa}
			\kappa(p)=\cot\theta_0
			\qquad
			\mbox{for every }p\in\partial M.
		\end{equation}
		
		By a rotation, we may assume that
		$$
		p=(\sin\theta_0,0,\cos\theta_0).
		$$
		Introducing the conformal coordinate
		$$
		z
		=
		\frac{\tan(\theta/2)}{\tan(\theta_0/2)}e^{i\varphi},
		$$
		it maps $M$ onto the closed unit disk, sends $p$ to $1$, and satisfies
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:spherical-cap-conformal-metric}
			g
			=
			\frac{4\tan^2(\theta_0/2)}
			{\left(1+\tan^2(\theta_0/2)|z|^2\right)^2}
			|dz|^2.
		\end{equation}
		One can check that the normalized Green function $G(z,p)$ with pole at $p$ defined in \eqref{eq:intro-green-function} is
		\begin{align}
			G(z,p)
			={}&
			-4\log|z-1|
			+
			\frac{1}{\sin^2(\theta_0/2)}
			\log\left(1+\tan^2\frac{\theta_0}{2}|z|^2\right)
			\notag\\
			&-
			\frac{1}{\sin^2(\theta_0/2)}
			+
			\frac{\cos^2(\theta_0/2)}{\sin^4(\theta_0/2)}
			\log\frac{1}{\cos^2(\theta_0/2)}.
			\label{eq:spherical-cap-green-function}
		\end{align}
		
		
		On $\partial M$, formula \eqref{eq:spherical-cap-green-function} becomes
		\begin{align}
			G(e^{i\varphi},p)
			={}&
			-4\log|e^{i\varphi}-1|+
			\frac{
				\log\dfrac{1}{\cos^2(\theta_0/2)}
				-
				\sin^2(\theta_0/2)
			}
			{\sin^4(\theta_0/2)}.
			\label{eq:spherical-cap-green-boundary}
		\end{align}
		If $r=d_g(x,p)$ and
		$$
		x=(\sin\theta_0\cos\varphi,
		\sin\theta_0\sin\varphi,
		\cos\theta_0)\in\partial M,
		$$
		then
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:spherical-cap-distance-relation}
		\sin\frac r2
			=
			\sin\theta_0\left|\sin\frac\varphi2\right|,\ \cos r
		=
		\cos^2\theta_0+\sin^2\theta_0\cos\varphi.
		\end{equation}
	
		
		Comparing \eqref{eq:spherical-cap-green-boundary} with
		$G(x,p)=-4\log r+A(p)+O(r)$, by \eqref{eq:spherical-cap-distance-relation}, we obtain
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:spherical-cap-regular-part}
			A(p)
			=
			4\log(\sin\theta_0)
			+
			\frac{
				\log\dfrac{1}{\cos^2(\theta_0/2)}
				-
				\sin^2(\theta_0/2)
			}
			{\sin^4(\theta_0/2)}.
		\end{equation}
		In particular, $A(p)$ is a constant on $\partial M$. Furthermore,
		by \eqref{eq:spherical-cap-green-boundary} and
		\eqref{eq:spherical-cap-regular-part}, we have
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:spherical-cap-boundary-green-density}
			e^{G(e^{i\varphi},p)/2}\,ds_g
			=
			\frac{e^{A(p)/2}}
			{4\sin\theta_0\sin^2(\varphi/2)}\,d\varphi.
		\end{equation}
		
		We identify $h|_{\partial M}$ with the corresponding $2\pi$-periodic
		function $h(\varphi)$, so that $h(0)=h(p)$. For sufficiently small
		$\delta>0$, let $\varphi_\delta\in(0,\pi)$ be determined by
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:spherical-cap-cutoff-relation}
			\sin\frac\delta2
			=
			\sin\theta_0\sin\frac{\varphi_\delta}{2}.
		\end{equation}
		Then \eqref{eq:spherical-cap-distance-relation} gives
		$$
		\partial M\cap\{r\geq\delta\}
		=
		\left\{e^{i\varphi}:
		\varphi_\delta\leq\varphi\leq2\pi-\varphi_\delta
		\right\}.
		$$
		Using \eqref{eq:spherical-cap-boundary-green-density} and
		$$
		\int_{\varphi_\delta}^{2\pi-\varphi_\delta}
		\frac{d\varphi}{\sin^2(\varphi/2)}
		=
		4\cot\frac{\varphi_\delta}{2},
		$$
		we obtain
		\begin{align}
			&\int_{\partial M\cap\{r\geq\delta\}}
			h(x)e^{G(x,p)/2}\,ds_g
			-
			\frac{2e^{A(p)/2}h(p)}{\delta}
			\notag\\
			&\quad=
			\frac{e^{A(p)/2}}{4\sin\theta_0}
			\int_{\varphi_\delta}^{2\pi-\varphi_\delta}
			\frac{h(\varphi)-h(0)}{\sin^2(\varphi/2)}\,d\varphi
			+
			e^{A(p)/2}h(0)
			\left[
			\frac{1}{\sin(\delta/2)}
			\sqrt{
				1-
				\frac{\sin^2(\delta/2)}{\sin^2\theta_0}
			}
			-
			\frac2\delta
			\right]\notag\\
			&\quad=
			\frac{e^{A(p)/2}}{4\sin\theta_0}
			\int_{\varphi_\delta}^{2\pi-\varphi_\delta}
			\frac{h(\varphi)-h(0)}{\sin^2(\varphi/2)}\,d\varphi+O(\delta).
			\label{eq:spherical-cap-finite-part-reduction}
		\end{align}
		

Since the metric induced on $\partial M$ is	$	\sin^2\theta_0\,d\varphi^2	$, by Proposition A.2 in \cite{Riviere}, we have $$(-\Delta_{\partial M})^{1/2}h(p)=\frac{1}{\sin\theta_0}(-\Delta_{S^1})^{1/2}h(p)=\frac{1}{4\pi\sin\theta_0}
			\operatorname{PV}
			\int_0^{2\pi}
			\frac{h(0)-h(\varphi)}
			{\sin^2(\varphi/2)}\,d\varphi.$$

Then
\begin{align}\label{equation:21}
			\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}
			\left[
			\int_{\partial M\cap\{r\geq\delta\}}
			h(x)e^{G(x,p)/2}\,ds_g
			-
			\frac{2e^{A(p)/2}h(p)}{\delta}
			\right]&
			=
			-\frac{e^{A(p)/2}}{4\sin\theta_0}
			\operatorname{PV}
			\int_0^{2\pi}
			\frac{h(0)-h(\varphi)}
			{\sin^2(\varphi/2)}\,d\varphi\notag\\&=
			-\pi e^{A(p)/2}
			(-\Delta_{\partial M})^{1/2}h(p).
		\end{align}
		
		
	
		
		Since $A(p)$ is constant on $\partial M$, we may take $p$ to be a
		maximum point of
		$$
		\rho\log K+2\rho'\log h
		\qquad\mbox{on }\partial M.
		$$
		Substituting \eqref{eq:spherical-cap-kappa} and \eqref{equation:21}
		 into Theorem \ref{thm:main-01} and Theorem \ref{thm:main-02},
			we get the first and second conclusions of Theorem \ref{thm:main-03}.
		
		In particular, assume that $K$ and $h$ are positive constants. Then
		$$
		K_\nu(p)=0,
		\qquad
		(-\Delta_{\partial M})^{1/2}h=0,
		$$
		and the sufficient condition \eqref{equation:22} reduces to
		$$
		-2\cot\theta_0>0,
		$$ which yields the third conclusion.

	=\frac{\rho}{2\pi}J_{2\pi,0}(u)
	+\left(1-\frac{\rho}{2\pi}\right)J_{0,2\pi}(u),
	$$ by the  Moser--Trudinger inequalities  \cite{ChangYang1988,LiLiu2005,Yang2006}
	$$
	J_{2\pi,0}(u)\geq-C,
	\qquad
	J_{0,2\pi}(u)\geq-C,
	\qquad u\in W^{1,2}(M),
	$$
	we get
	$$
	J_{\rho,\,2\pi-\rho}(u)\geq-C,\ \ u\in W^{1,2}(M),\ \rho\in[0,2\pi].
	$$
 Therefore,
	\begin{equation}\label{equation:18}
	\widehat J(u,\rho)\geq-C,
	\qquad
	\widehat J_t(u,\rho)
	\geq\frac{t}{2}\int_M|\nabla_g u|^2\,dv_g-C,\ \ u\in W^{1,2}(M),\ \rho\in[0,2\pi].
	\end{equation}
	 In particular, this implies the functional $\widehat J_t(u,\rho)$ is coercive for any fixed $t>0$ and the following infimum  exists		$$
	m:=\inf_{\substack{u\in W^{1,2}(M)\\0\leq\rho\leq2\pi}}
	\widehat J(u,\rho).
	$$
By the classical variational method, we can assume  $\widehat J_t(u,\rho)$ admits a joint global minimizer
	$(u_t,\rho_t)$. Then
	\begin{equation*}
		\begin{aligned}
			m&\leq\widehat J(u_t,\rho_t)
			\leq\widehat J_t(u_t,\rho_t)\leq\widehat J(v,\rho)
			+\frac{t}{2}\int_M|\nabla_gv|^2\,dv_g,\ \ \forall\  (v,\rho)\in W^{1,2}(M)\times[0,2\pi].
		\end{aligned}
	\end{equation*} That is $$m=\lim_{t\to 0}\widehat J(u_t,\rho_t)
			= \lim_{t\to 0}\widehat J_t(u_t,\rho_t).$$
	
	For fixed $t$, as $s\downarrow0$, we have
	$$
	\begin{aligned}
		\widehat J_t(u_t,s)-\widehat J_t(u_t,0)
		&=2s\log s+O(s),\\
		\widehat J_t(u_t,2\pi-s)-\widehat J_t(u_t,2\pi)
		&=4s\log s+O(s).
	\end{aligned}
	$$
	Thus minimality excludes both endpoints, and
	$0<\rho_t<2\pi$.
	
	The first variation in $u$ gives
	$$
	\begin{cases}
		\displaystyle
		-(1+t)\Delta_g u_t+2
		=2\rho_t\frac{Ke^{u_t}}{\int_MKe^{u_t}\,dv_g},
		&\text{in }M,\\[1.2em]
		\displaystyle
		(1+t)\partial_\nu u_t
		=2(2\pi-\rho_t)
		\frac{he^{u_t/2}}{\int_{\partial M}he^{u_t/2}\,ds_g},
		&\text{on }\partial M.
	\end{cases}
	$$
	Since the regularizing term is independent of $\rho$, the
	first variation in $\rho$ gives
	$\partial_\rho\widehat J(u_t,\rho_t)=0$. That is
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:joint-perturbed-compatibility}
		\frac{
			\left(\displaystyle\int_{\partial M}
			he^{u_t/2}\,ds_g\right)^2}
		{\displaystyle\int_MKe^{u_t}\,dv_g}
		=\frac{(2\pi-\rho_t)^2}{\rho_t}.
	\end{equation}
	Set
	$$
	w_t=u_t+
	\log\frac{\rho_t}
	{(1+t)\displaystyle\int_MKe^{u_t}\,dv_g}.
	$$
	Then \eqref{eq:joint-perturbed-compatibility} and the equation
	for $u_t$ yield
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:joint-perturbed-equation}
		\begin{cases}
			\displaystyle
			-\Delta_gw_t+\frac{2}{1+t}=2Ke^{w_t},
			&\text{in }M,\\[6pt]
			\displaystyle
			\partial_\nu w_t
			=\frac{2h}{\sqrt{1+t}}e^{w_t/2},
			&\text{on }\partial M.
		\end{cases}
	\end{equation}
	Moreover,
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:joint-perturbed-masses}
		\begin{aligned}
			\int_MKe^{w_t}\,dv_g=\frac{\rho_t}{1+t},\ \
			\int_{\partial M}\frac{h}{\sqrt{1+t}}
			e^{w_t/2}\,ds_g=\frac{2\pi-\rho_t}{1+t}.
		\end{aligned}
	\end{equation}
	
	
	
	Passing to a subsequence, assume that
	$\rho_t\to\rho_*\in[0,2\pi]$ as $t\downarrow0$. Then we have to consider the following two cases.

\

\noindent\textbf{Case 1.} The sequence $w_t$ is uniformly bounded above.

\

By standard elliptic estimates and
\eqref{eq:joint-perturbed-masses}, after passing to a subsequence,
we have
$$
w_t\longrightarrow w_*
\qquad\text{in }C^2(M).
$$
Passing to the limit in \eqref{eq:joint-perturbed-equation}
as $t\downarrow0$, we obtain
$$
\begin{cases}
	-\Delta_gw_*+2=2Ke^{w_*},
	&\text{in }M,\\
	\partial_\nu w_*=2he^{w_*/2},
	&\text{on }\partial M.
\end{cases}
$$
Thus $w_*$ is a smooth solution of the prescribed curvature
problem.

\


\noindent\textbf{Case 2.} The sequence $w_t$ blows up.

\


In this case, we will show that the infimum $m$ will be attained by $(u_*,\rho_*)\in W^{1,2}(M)\times (0,2\pi)$. We divide the remaining proof into the following steps.
	
\

	\noindent\textbf{Step 1:} The infimum $m$  satisfies $m<4\pi-8\pi\log\Phi(p)$.

\

	On the standard hemisphere, we have $A=4\log2-2$ and
	$\kappa=0$. Taking
	$$
	\rho_p=2\pi\left(
	1-\frac{h(p)}{\sqrt{K(p)+h(p)^2}}
	\right)\in(0,2\pi),
	$$
	and the test function $\phi_{\epsilon,\delta}$ centered at
	$p$ in \eqref{eq:test-function}, with parameters $(\rho_p,2\pi-\rho_p)$, by Proposition \ref{prop:01}
	and \eqref{equation:22} with
	$\theta_0=\pi/2$, we obtain
	$$
	\begin{aligned}
		\widehat J(\phi_{\epsilon,\delta},\rho_p)
		={}&4\pi-8\pi\log\Phi(p)-\frac{4\pi}{\Phi(p)\sqrt{K(p)}}
		\left[
		K_2(p)-2\Phi(p)(-\Delta_{\partial M})^{1/2}h(p)
		\right]\sqrt{\epsilon}\\
		&+O(\delta\sqrt{\epsilon})
		+o(\sqrt{\epsilon}).
	\end{aligned}
	$$
	By \eqref{eq:joint-boundary-condition}, first choosing
	$\delta>0$ sufficiently small and then $\epsilon>0$
	sufficiently small, we obtain
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:joint-strict-blow-up-level}
		m\leq\widehat J(\phi_{\epsilon,\delta},\rho_p)
		<4\pi-8\pi\log\Phi(p).
	\end{equation}
	
	\
	
\noindent\textbf{Step 2:} There exists $\rho_*\in (0,2\pi)$ such that $m=\inf_{u\in W^{1,2}(M)}\widehat J(u,\rho_*)$.

\
	
	


Passing to a subsequence, assume that
$$
\max_M w_t\longrightarrow+\infty,
\qquad
\rho_t\longrightarrow\rho_*\in[0,2\pi].
$$
Suppose $w_t$ blows up at $q$. Since
$$
\int_M2Ke^{w_t}\,dv_g
=\frac{2\rho_t}{1+t}\leq4\pi,
$$
it must be that $q\in\partial M$. Suppose $w_t(x_t)=\max_Mw_t=\lambda_t$. Setting $$U_t(x):=w_t (x_t+\delta_t x)+2\log\delta_t,\ \ where\ \ \delta_t=e^{-\frac{\lambda_t}{2}}.$$
By the argument in Section \ref{sec:blow-up-analysis}, we know $U_t$ converges strongly to $U$ in $C^2_{loc}(\mathbb R^2_+)$ where
$$
\begin{cases}
	-\Delta U=2K(q)e^U,
	&\text{in }\mathbb R^2_+,\\
	\partial_\nu U=2h(q)e^{U/2},
	&\text{on }\partial\mathbb R^2_+.
\end{cases}
$$
By \eqref{eq:joint-perturbed-masses},
we have
\begin{equation}\label{inequ:01}
	\int_{\mathbb R^2_+}K(q)e^U\,dx
	\leq\rho_*,\ \
	\int_{\mathbb R}h(q)e^{U(x_1,0)/2}\,dx_1
	\leq2\pi-\rho_*.
\end{equation}
The classification result in \cite{Li-Zhu} that
$$
\int_{\mathbb R^2_+}K(q)e^U\,dx
+\int_{\mathbb R}h(q)e^{U(x_1,0)/2}\,dx_1=2\pi,
$$
yields that both
inequalities in \eqref{inequ:01} are in fact equalities.

We now compute $\rho_*$. By \cite{Li-Zhu}, we have
$$
U(x)
=\log\frac{4\lambda^2}
{K(q)\left[
	\lambda^2+x_1^2+
	\left(x_2+\frac{h(q)\lambda}{\sqrt{K(q)}}\right)^2
	\right]^2},
\qquad \lambda=\frac{2\sqrt{K(q)}}{K(q)+h^2(q)}.
$$
Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:joint-limiting-mass}
	\rho_*=2\pi-\int_{\partial \mathbb R^2_+}h(q)e^{\frac{1}{2}U(x)}dx_1
	=2\pi\left(
	1-\frac{h(q)}{\sqrt{K(q)+h(q)^2}}
	\right)\in(0,2\pi).
\end{equation}


Noting that
$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial \rho}\widehat J(u_t,\rho_t)=\frac{\partial}{\partial \rho}\widehat J_t(u_t,\rho_t)=0,\ \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \rho^2}\widehat J(u_t,\rho_t)=\frac{4\pi+2\rho_t}{\rho_t(2\pi-\rho_t)}
$$
 and
$\rho_t\to\rho_*\in(0,2\pi)$, by Taylor's expansion, we get
$$
\widehat J(u_t,\rho_*)
=\widehat J(u_t,\rho_t)
+O(|\rho_t-\rho_*|^2)
\longrightarrow m,\ as \ t\to 0.
$$
Hence
$$
m\leq
\inf_{u\in W^{1,2}(M)}\widehat J(u,\rho_*)
\leq\widehat J(u_t,\rho_*)\longrightarrow m,
$$
and therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:joint-fixed-slice-infimum}
	\inf_{u\in W^{1,2}(M)}\widehat J(u,\rho_*)=m.
\end{equation}

\

\noindent\textbf{Step 3:} There exists
$u_*\in W^{1,2}(M)$ such that
$$
\widehat J(u_*,\rho_*)
=\inf_{u\in W^{1,2}(M)}\widehat J(u,\rho_*)=m.
$$

\

Let $u_\epsilon$
be a minimizer of
$
J_{\rho_*-\epsilon,\,2\pi-\rho_*},
$
normalized by \eqref{equation:03}.

\

\noindent\textbf{Claim:} Passing to a subsequence, there holds
$$
u_\epsilon\longrightarrow u_*
\qquad\text{strongly in }W^{1,2}(M).
$$
Then $u_*$
minimizes $J_{\rho_*,\,2\pi-\rho_*}$. Since
$\widehat J(\cdot,\rho_*)$ differs from
$J_{\rho_*,\,2\pi-\rho_*}$ only by a constant,
\eqref{eq:joint-fixed-slice-infimum} gives
$$
\widehat J(u_*,\rho_*)
=\inf_{u\in W^{1,2}(M)}\widehat J(u,\rho_*)=m.
$$

\

We prove the claim by a contradiction argument. Otherwise, $u_\epsilon$ blows up. By
Proposition \ref{prop:lower-bound} and the definition of $\widehat J(u,\rho_*)$,  noting that $A=4\log2-2$ for $M=\mathbb S^2_+$, we have
\begin{align*}
\widehat J(u,\rho_*)&=\lim_{\epsilon\to 0} J_{\rho_*-\epsilon,2\pi-\rho_*}(u)+2\rho_*\log\rho_*
		+4(2\pi-\rho_*)\log(2\pi-\rho_*)+2\rho_*\\
&\geq \lim_{\epsilon\to 0} J_{\rho_*-\epsilon,2\pi-\rho_*}(u_\epsilon)+2\rho_*\log\rho_*
		+4(2\pi-\rho_*)\log(2\pi-\rho_*)+2\rho_*\\
&\geq \min_{z\in\partial M}L(\rho_*,z)
\end{align*} where
$$
\begin{aligned}
	L(\rho,z)
	={}&4\pi-2(4\pi-\rho)\log(4\pi-\rho)
	+2\rho\log\rho\\
	&+4(2\pi-\rho)\log(2\pi-\rho)
	-2\rho\log K(z)-4(2\pi-\rho)\log h(z).
\end{aligned}
$$
Thus,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:joint-fixed-mass-threshold}
	m=\inf_{u\in W^{1,2}(M)}\widehat J(u,\rho_*)
	\geq\min_{z\in\partial M}L(\rho_*,z).
\end{equation}


For every fixed $z\in\partial M$, a direct computation gives
$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial\rho} L(\rho,z)
=2\log\frac{\rho(4\pi-\rho)h(z)^2}
{(2\pi-\rho)^2K(z)},\ \ \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \rho^2} L(\rho,z)>0.
$$
Thus the function $L(\cdot,z)$ has a unique minimum at
$$
\rho_z=2\pi\left(
1-\frac{h(z)}{\sqrt{K(z)+h(z)^2}}
\right).
$$
Therefore, by the choice of $p$, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:joint-optimal-blow-up-level}
	L(\rho,z)\geq L(\rho_z,z)=4\pi-8\pi\log\Phi(z)
	\geq4\pi-8\pi\log\Phi(p)
\end{equation}
for every $0<\rho<2\pi$ and $z\in\partial M$.
Then \eqref{eq:joint-fixed-mass-threshold}  gives
$$
m\geq4\pi-8\pi\log\Phi(p),
$$
 which is a contradiction to \eqref{eq:joint-strict-blow-up-level}.       Thus we proved the claim.

Consequently, there exists $u_*\in W^{1,2}(M)$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:joint-limit-minimality}
	\widehat J(u_*,\rho_*)
	=\inf_{u\in W^{1,2}(M)}\widehat J(u,\rho_*)=m,
	\qquad 0<\rho_*<2\pi.
\end{equation}

body_md:
Let $\overline{\mathbb D}$ be the closed unit disk with the metric
	$$
	g=e^\varphi(dx_1^2+dx_2^2),
	\qquad
	\varphi(x)=2\log\frac{2}{1+|x|^2}.
	$$
	Consider the isometric map
	$$
	F(x_1,x_2)
	=\frac{1}{1+|x|^2}
	\left(2x_1,2x_2,1-|x|^2\right): (\overline{\mathbb D},g)\to (\mathbb S^2_+,g_{\mathbb S^2}).
	$$
	It is easy to see that
	$$
	F^{-1}(y_1,y_2,y_3)
	=\left(\frac{y_1}{1+y_3},\frac{y_2}{1+y_3}\right),\ \ \left\langle
	\frac{\partial F}{\partial x_i},
	\frac{\partial F}{\partial x_j}
	\right\rangle_{\mathbb R^3}
	=\frac{4}{(1+|x|^2)^2}\delta_{ij},
	\ \ i,j=1,2.
	$$
	
	
	
Denote $\nu$ and $\nu_g$  the outward unit normal vectors to
$\partial\mathbb D$ with respect to the Euclidean metric
and $g$ respectively. Since $\varphi=0$ on
$\partial\mathbb D$, we have
$$
\nu_g=e^{-\varphi/2}\nu=\nu
\qquad\text{on }\partial\mathbb D.
$$
Set
$$
\widetilde K=K\circ F^{-1},
\ \
\widetilde h=h\circ F^{-1},\ \ \widetilde\Phi
=\widetilde h+\sqrt{\widetilde h^2+\widetilde K}.
$$
Since $H=h$ on $\partial\mathbb D$, we have
$$
\widetilde\Phi\circ F=\Phi
\qquad\text{on }\partial\mathbb D.
$$
Hence $F(p)$ is a maximum point of $\widetilde\Phi$ on
$\partial M$ and
$$
\widetilde K_2(F(p))
=-\partial_{\nu_g}K(p)
=-\partial_\nu K(p).
$$

Recall that $H$ satisfies
$$
\begin{cases}
	\Delta H=0,
	&\text{in }\mathbb D,\\
	H=h,
	&\text{on }\partial\mathbb D,
\end{cases}
$$
where $\Delta$ is the Euclidean Laplacian.
By \cite[formula~(A.3) and Lemma~A.1]{CabreCsatoMas},
$$
(-\Delta_{\mathbb S^1})^{1/2}h=\partial_\nu H
\qquad\text{on }\partial\mathbb D.
$$




Differentiating $\Phi=H+\sqrt{H^2+K}$ in the Euclidean
outward normal direction, we obtain
$$
2\sqrt{H^2+K}\,\partial_\nu\Phi
=\partial_\nu K+2\Phi\,\partial_\nu H
\qquad\text{on }\partial\mathbb D.
$$
Recalling that
$$
\widetilde K_2(F(p))=-\partial_\nu K(p),
\ \
\widetilde\Phi \circ F=\Phi,\ \ \widetilde h\circ F=h
$$ and noting that $$
\left[
(-\Delta_{\partial M})^{1/2}\widetilde h
\right]\circ F
=(-\Delta_{\mathbb S^1})^{1/2}h
=\partial_\nu H
\qquad\text{on }\partial\mathbb D,
$$
we have
$$
\begin{aligned}
	\widetilde K_2(F(p))
	-2\widetilde\Phi(F(p))
	\left[
	(-\Delta_{\partial M})^{1/2}\widetilde h
	\right](F(p))
	&
	=-\partial_\nu K(p)-2\Phi(p)\partial_\nu H(p)\\
	&
	=-2\sqrt{h(p)^2+K(p)}\,\partial_\nu\Phi(p)>0.
\end{aligned}
$$
Since $F(p)$ is a maximum point of $\widetilde\Phi$ on
$\partial M$, all the assumptions of
Theorem~\ref{thm:main-05} are satisfied.
Then there exists a solution
$w\in C^\infty(\overline{\mathbb D})$ to
$$
\begin{cases}
	-\Delta_gw+2=2Ke^w,
	&\text{in }\mathbb D,\\
	\partial_{\nu_g}w=2he^{w/2},
	&\text{on }\partial\mathbb D,
\end{cases}
$$
where $g=e^\varphi(dx_1^2+dx_2^2)$.


Using the facts that
$$
-\Delta\varphi
=\frac{8}{(1+|x|^2)^2}
=2e^\varphi
\ \ \text{in }\mathbb D, \  \ \varphi=0,
\ \
\partial_\nu\varphi=-2
\ \ \text{on }\partial\mathbb D,
$$
it is easy to see that $u=w+\varphi$ satisfies
$$
\begin{cases}
	-\Delta u=2Ke^u,
	&\text{in }\mathbb D,\\
	\partial_\nu u+2=2he^{u/2},
	&\text{on }\partial\mathbb D,
\end{cases}
$$ which is the desired solution.

body_md:
\label{lem:03}		
		Let $(M,g)$ be a smooth Riemann surface, and let
		$\gamma:(-\epsilon_0,\epsilon_0)\to M$ be a $C^4$ curve
		parametrized by arc length. Set $p=\gamma(0)$, choose a smooth unit
		normal vector field $\nu(s)$ along $\gamma$, and define the signed
		geodesic curvature $\kappa(s)$ by
		$$
		\nabla_{\dot{\gamma}}\dot{\gamma}=\kappa(s)\nu(s).
		$$
		Let $e_1=\dot{\gamma}(0)$ and $e_2=\nu(0)$, and define geodesic normal
		coordinates centered at $p$ by
		$$
		(x_1,x_2)\longmapsto\exp_p(x_1e_1+x_2e_2).
		$$
		Then, for $|x_1|$ sufficiently small, $\gamma$ can be written as
		$x_2=f(x_1)$, where
		$$
		f(x_1)
		=
		\frac{\kappa(0)}{2}x_1^2
		+
		\frac{\kappa'(0)}{6}x_1^3
		+
		O(x_1^4).
		$$
		Here $\kappa'(0)=\left.\frac{d\kappa}{ds}\right|_{s=0}$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $\gamma(s)=(x_1(s),x_2(s))$ in the above coordinates. Since
		$\gamma(0)=p$, $e_1=\dot{\gamma}(0)$, and $e_2=\nu(0)$, we have
		$$
		x_1(0)=x_2(0)=0,
		\qquad
		x_1'(0)=1,
		\qquad
		x_2'(0)=0.
		$$
		Moreover, geodesic normal coordinates satisfy
		$$
		g_{ij}(p)=\delta_{ij},
		\qquad
		\Gamma_{ij}^m(p)=0,
		$$ where $\Gamma_{ij}^m$ is the Christoffel symbols.
		
		Since
		$\dot{\gamma}=\sum_{i=1}^2x_i'\partial_{x_i}$, the local coordinate
		formula for the covariant derivative gives
		$$
		\left(\nabla_{\dot{\gamma}}\dot{\gamma}\right)^m
		=
		x_m''
		+
		\sum_{i,j=1}^2
		\Gamma_{ij}^m(\gamma(s))x_i'x_j'.
		$$
		Evaluating at $s=0$, all Christoffel symbols vanish, and hence
		$$
		\left(\nabla_{\dot{\gamma}}\dot{\gamma}\right)^m(p)
		=
		x_m''(0).
		$$
		Since
		$\nabla_{\dot{\gamma}}\dot{\gamma}(p)=\kappa(0)e_2$, it follows that
		$$
		x_1''(0)=0,
		\qquad
		x_2''(0)=\kappa(0).
		$$
		
		Metric compatibility and
		$\langle\dot{\gamma},\nu\rangle_g=0$ imply
		$\nabla_{\dot{\gamma}}\nu=-\kappa\dot{\gamma}$. Therefore,
		$$
		\nabla_{\dot{\gamma}}
		\left(\nabla_{\dot{\gamma}}\dot{\gamma}\right)
		=
		\kappa'\nu-\kappa^2\dot{\gamma}.
		$$
		At $s=0$, its two coordinate components are
		$-\kappa(0)^2$ and $\kappa'(0)$.
		
		On the other hand, differentiating the coordinate expression for
		$\nabla_{\dot{\gamma}}\dot{\gamma}$ and using
		$x_1'(0)=1$, $x_2'(0)=0$, and $\Gamma_{ij}^m(p)=0$, we obtain
		$$
		\left[
		\nabla_{\dot{\gamma}}
		\left(\nabla_{\dot{\gamma}}\dot{\gamma}\right)
		\right]^m(p)
		=
		x_m'''(0)
		+
		\partial_1\Gamma_{11}^m(p).
		$$
		The coordinate curve $t\mapsto(t,0)$ is a geodesic, so its geodesic
		equation gives $\Gamma_{11}^m(t,0)=0$. Consequently,
		$\partial_1\Gamma_{11}^m(p)=0$, and hence
		$$
		x_1'''(0)=-\kappa(0)^2,
		\qquad
		x_2'''(0)=\kappa'(0).
		$$
		
		Since $x_1'(0)=1$, the inverse function theorem allows us to write
		$x_2=f(x_1)$. Differentiating
		$x_2(s)=f(x_1(s))$ at $s=0$ gives
		$$
		f(0)=f'(0)=0,
		\qquad
		f''(0)=\kappa(0),
		\qquad
		f'''(0)=\kappa'(0).
		$$
		The conclusion follows from Taylor's theorem.
